The Grey-backed shrike (Lanius tephronotus) is a medium-sized passerine found across the montane scrublands of the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau. Field measurements of freshly laid eggs indicate an initial wet weight of approximately 4.4 grams [Ww0 = approximately 4.4 grams], a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves required for embryonic development during the long incubation period. Neonates emerge from the shell at a markedly reduced mass, with the wet weight at birth recorded at 3.6 grams [Wwb = 3.6 grams], representing a modest proportion of the egg's total mass and suggesting efficient conversion of yolk to embryonic tissue. When incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the age at birth, or hatching interval, spans approximately 14.5 days [ab = approximately 14.5 days], a duration consistent with the developmental rates observed in other Lanius species. This relatively short incubation period, coupled with the small size of the hatchlings, is typical of altricial songbirds that rely heavily on biparental provisioning during the initial weeks of life.

Adults of this species exhibit a pronounced sexual size dimorphism, which is evident in their asymptotic body masses. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of 48.5 grams [Wwi = 48.5 grams], while males attain a slightly larger ultimate wet weight of 49.2 grams [Wwi = 49.2 grams], a pattern that reverses the typical avian trend of larger females. This modest but consistent difference may be linked to the species' territorial and predatory habits, where males engage in vigorous defense of hunting perches and nest sites. Under the thermal conditions typical of the breeding season, which average 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum documented longevity reaches approximately 10.1 years [am = approximately 10.1 years]. This lifespan is notably extended for a shrike of this body size, suggesting that the harsh, high-altitude environment may select for slower senescence and increased annual survival.

The reproductive biology of the Grey-backed shrike is characterized by a modest yet consistent output. Females typically lay 4.9 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4.9 eggs per clutch], a clutch size that aligns with the modal value for temperate-zone Lanius species. They routinely produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], allowing for a substantial annual reproductive effort. The daily reproduction rate is not expressed as a rate but is implicit in the combination of clutch size and frequency, reflecting a strategy that balances the demands of incubation and chick rearing against the brief, productive summer months of their montane habitat. During the breeding season, when ambient temperatures hover around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at first brood, or the onset of successful reproduction, is attained at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth]. This deferred first breeding, occurring roughly one year after hatching, is typical of species that invest heavily in territorial establishment and pre-breeding foraging experience.

Timing of developmental milestones in this species follows a predictable sequence under the elevated metabolic conditions of the active season. At a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at 48 days since birth [tp = 48 days since birth]. This relatively early attainment of sexual maturity in a physiological sense contrasts with the much later age at first successful reproduction, indicating a significant gap between physical readiness and the ecological opportunity to breed. The time since birth at fledging, representing the age at which young birds achieve sustained flight, occurs at 16 days since birth [tx = 16 days since birth] under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid fledging period, among the shortest recorded for shrikes, is an adaptation to the short alpine growing season, enabling juveniles to depart the nest and begin independent foraging before the onset of harsh autumn weather.

Comparative studies within the Laniidae highlight several distinctive life-history traits of this high-altitude specialist. The initial wet weight of approximately 4.4 grams [Ww0 = approximately 4.4 grams] at oviposition is relatively high for a bird of this adult size, likely reflecting the need for a well-provisioned egg in a cold, oxygen-thin environment. The wet weight at birth of 3.6 grams [Wwb = 3.6 grams] represents a hatchling that is well-developed and capable of thermoregulation within days of emergence. The age at birth of approximately 14.5 days [ab = approximately 14.5 days] at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] is similar to that of other montane passerines. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the species' maximum lifespan of 3,686 days [am = 3,686 days] stands in contrast to its smaller congener, the Red-backed Shrike, which seldom exceeds five years. Furthermore, the balanced sexual dimorphism in ultimate wet weight, 48.5 grams [Wwi = 48.5 grams] for females and 49.2 grams [Wwi = 49.2 grams] for males, suggests divergent selective pressures on foraging ecology and parental roles in this resource-poor environment.
